prompt:
What is the fully simplified growth description of the exact operation count below, with fixed coefficients and dominated terms removed?

```formula essential
T(n) = 4n^3 + 20n^2 log(n) + 1000
where
T: the running-time function, in counted basic steps
log: the base-2 logarithm
n: the input size
In words: The running-time model adds a cubic term, a quadratic-times-log term and a fixed overhead.
```

options.explanation: True but not simplified: the quadratic-times-log term is dominated by the cubic term.
Also technically true, but fixed coefficients can be absorbed into the bound's constant multipliers. Θ(4n^3) and Θ(n^3) are the same set. Here n is the input item count.
Correct. The ratio of cubic growth to quadratic-times-log growth is unbounded, so the cubic term dominates; fixed coefficients and constant overhead vanish.
This picks the most elaborate term instead of the fastest-growing one. The logarithm grows more slowly than the extra factor of n in the cubic term.

workedExample: Compare growth, not visual complexity. A cubic term eventually outgrows a quadratic term multiplied by a logarithm. Fixed coefficients and fixed overhead change values but not that dominant growth. With n denoting input size, the fully simplified description is Θ(n³).

prompt: Which of these statements are **true**? Select all that apply. (n is the input size; O is an upper bound on growth, Θ a tight bound; log2 and log10 are logarithms to base 2 and base 10.)

options.text: Linear has a quadratic upper bound
options.explanation: True. A quadratic upper bound covers linear work.

options.text: Quadratic has a linear upper bound
options.explanation: False. The ratio grows without limit, so no fixed linear multiplier suffices.

options.text: Twice input plus five has tight linear growth
options.explanation: True. Fixed linear multiples squeeze the function.

options.text: Base-two and base-ten logs have the same tight growth
options.explanation: True. Changing a log base multiplies the value by a fixed factor.

options.text: Base-three exponential has a base-two exponential upper bound
options.explanation: False. Changing the exponential base leaves an unbounded ratio.

workedExample: A linear cost fits beneath a quadratic upper bound, but not conversely. A fixed multiple of input plus fixed setup still grows linearly. Fixed logarithm bases differ by a constant multiplier. Exponential bases differ by a ratio that keeps growing, so the faster base cannot be hidden in one fixed multiplier.

prompt: Which listed function does **not** have an O(2^n) upper bound? Here n is the input size, and O means an eventual upper bound up to a fixed factor.

options.text: Base two to one more than input
options.explanation: This has the bound: increasing the exponent by one gives only a fixed factor of two.

options.text: Base two to input, plus input’s fifth power
options.explanation: This has the bound: a fixed fifth power is eventually negligible beside the base-two exponential.
This has the bound: a fixed tenth power loses to an exponential eventually, even if it is large for small inputs.
Correct: this does not have the bound. Its ratio to the comparison exponential remains exponential.

workedExample: An extra fixed amount in the exponent contributes a fixed multiplier. Fixed polynomials are eventually dominated by the base-two exponential. Changing from base two to base four instead introduces another growing exponential factor, so that candidate has no base-two exponential upper bound.
